(e) Minimax: since v/(k D(v)) is monotone in v the worst error sits at the endpoints, so minimax k = (A+B)/2 with A = v1/D(v1), B = v2/D(v2): 1.8494/0.1997, 4.2576/0.4789, 3.7380/0.6844, 11.4014/0.8702, margins 0.40489, 0.21582, 5.80252, 1.76392, all equal to the author's golden-section results; LS-never-underestimates checked on 2,379 further ranges (0 exceptions). run.py output is byte-identical to experiments/results.txt. evidence.craft: Read src/friction_twin/model.py (106 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, figure.py. Small, readable, pure functions. Defects: real_stop_time/real_stop_distance divide by b and c (model.py:9, :14), so pure Coulomb friction (b = 0, the case where a viscous twin is worst) raises ZeroDivisionError rather than returning m v0^2/(2c); crossover_speed silently returns None when k <= b (model.py:69); minimax_k runs a 120-step golden section over a 400-point grid when the optimum has a two-line closed form (endpoint equioscillation, since the ratio is monotone), and its unimodality is asserted in a docstring, not shown; run.py uses 'from friction_twin.model import *'. 3.
evidence.claims: Backed: every number in README.md:3 and paper/whitepaper.md results 1-6 is in results.txt and reproduced independently; limitations (one DOF, noiseless, uniform speeds, simulated 'real') are stated; no-affiliation note in README. Not backed: 'a twin that models friction as viscous only ... is the default in many simulators' (whitepaper.md:6) has no citation, and common engines (MuJoCo frictionloss, ODE/Gazebo, Bullet) model Coulomb friction; 'Negative result' (README:3, whitepaper.md:16) frames a textbook consequence of fitting a one-parameter linear model to an affine law as a finding, and the paper never says that the stopping-distance closed form, the omitted-intercept bias of LS through the origin, or the A + Bv coast-down fit are standard; SAE J2263/J1263 coast-down practice is not cited. 2.
evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: Armstrong-Helouvry, Dupont & Canudas de Wit (1994) survey and Olsson et al. (1998) (both cited) treat Coulomb+viscous(+Stribeck, LuGre) models and their identification; coast-down road-load testing (SAE J1263/J2263) fits F = A + Bv + Cv^2 from coast-down logs, i.e. the paper's affine repair plus aero; the closed-form coast-down distance under constant plus linear drag is a standard dynamics exercise; the LS bias b + c E[v]/E[v^2] is the textbook omitted-intercept bias. The new content is the minimax-viscous-gain table and the observation that LS is conservative inside its range, both minor. A researcher could not build a paper on it; as teaching material for 'don't drop the Coulomb term' it is sound. 2.
evidence.domain: Against friction-identification practice: identifying Coulomb plus viscous (and Stribeck) from constant-velocity sweeps or coast-down is the standard (Armstrong-Helouvry 1994; Canudas de Wit LuGre 1995); nobody in practice fits a through-origin viscous gain when a coast-down shows a nonzero intercept. Departures a practitioner would flag: speeds are assumed uniform on [v1, v2], but a coast-down logger samples uniformly in time, which weights low speeds more; my time-sampled LS gives k = 1.2454 on [1,3] (vs 1.2308), 3.5216 on [0.05,0.3] (vs 3.4419), 1.0923 on [0.2,10] (vs 1.0750), so table 2 is not the gain a real coast-down would give (the assumption is disclosed, its effect is not); no noise, so the 'affine fit recovers (b, c) exactly' is trivially exact; no Stribeck or stiction, which is where viscous twins actually fail in robotics. 2.

verdict: Numerically right and fully reproducible: run.py regenerates results.txt byte for byte, and my own stdlib script (own (x, v) RK4 with event bisection, Simpson quadrature, exact rational moments, analytic minimax by endpoint equioscillation) reproduces the stopping distances to 2.3e-13, the fitted gains 1.230769/1.725806/1.035714/3.441860, the ratios, the crossover 7.3395, the twin times 6.51/12.12/17.73 s and every minimax and margin figure. It does not meet the bar: verification 2 (5 of 6 seeded mutations survive, every test uses m = 1, minimax untested) and claims 2 (an uncited 'default in many simulators' premise, and textbook facts, the coast-down closed form, the omitted-intercept LS bias and the A + Bv road-load fit standard in SAE J1263/J2263 coast-down testing, framed as results and a 'negative result'). For a controls or system-identification researcher there is nothing new to build on; it is sound teaching material on why the Coulomb term matters.
